items.stem: What is an expenditure-switching policy?
options: A policy that raises government spending on imports
A policy that switches spending from consumption to saving
A policy that changes the relative prices of imports and domestic goods so that spending switches to domestic output
A policy that reduces total spending in the economy
items.answer: A policy that changes the relative prices of imports and domestic goods so that spending switches to domestic output
items.markingKey: Tariffs, quotas, devaluation, export subsidies.

items.stem: Explain how a devaluation can be used to reduce a current account deficit.
items.answer: Exports become cheaper in foreign currency and imports dearer in domestic currency; spending switches from imports to domestic goods and foreign demand for exports rises, improving the current account if the Marshall–Lerner condition holds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relative price changes; 1 mark: spending switches; 1 mark: Marshall–Lerner/elasticities [3]

items.stem: Explain two limitations of using tariffs to correct a current account deficit.
items.answer: Retaliation reduces exports; higher prices and inflation; inefficiency in protected industries; demand for imports may be price inelastic; may break WTO rules.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two limitations, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: The government of Kestria raises income tax rates to reduce consumer spending. Which type of policy to correct a current account deficit is this?
items.answer: Expenditure-reducing policy
items.markingKey: Expenditure-reducing policy: lower disposable income reduces total spending, including on imports.

items.stem: Classify each policy as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side, and explain how it could reduce a current account deficit. (i) Esteria introduces a quota on imported cars. (ii) The government of Esteria funds training to raise productivity in export industries.
items.answer: (i) Expenditure-switching policy: limits imports so spending switches to domestic cars. (ii) Supply-side policy: improves competitiveness in the long run.
items.markingKey: (i) Expenditure-switching policy [1]; explanation [1] (ii) Supply-side policy [1]; explanation [1] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: Jovania has a current account deficit of 7% of GDP, unemployment of 11% and inflation of 8%. The finance minister proposes higher income tax to cut spending; the central bank prefers to let the naira depreciate; business leaders call for tariffs on imported consumer goods; economists argue that only supply-side reforms will solve the problem. The marginal propensity to import is 0.2. (a) Classify each of the four proposals as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side. (b) Calculate the fall in national income needed to reduce imports by $6bn.
items.answer: (a) Higher income tax: expenditure-reducing; depreciation and tariffs: expenditure-switching; supply-side reforms: supply-side. (b) ΔY = 6/0.2 = $30bn.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Higher income tax: expenditure-reducing; depreciation and tariffs: expenditure-switching; supply-side reforms: supply-side. [2] (b) Credit: ΔY = 6/0.2 = $30bn. [2]

items.stem: Which is an expenditure-switching policy?
items.answer: A devaluation of the currency
items.markingKey: Changes relative prices of imports and exports.

items.stem: Explain the difference between expenditure-switching and expenditure-reducing policies.
items.answer: Expenditure-switching changes relative prices so that spending moves from imports to domestic goods; expenditure-reducing lowers total spending (AD), which reduces imports as a by-product.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: switching relative prices; 1 mark: reducing total spending [2]

items.stem: Tomás makes the following statement: ‘A devaluation of the kwacha will improve Ostrelia’s current account immediately.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: In the short run demand is price inelastic, so the current account may worsen first (J-curve); improvement depends on the Marshall–Lerner condition.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – In the short run demand is price inelastic, so the current account may worsen first (J-curve); improvement depends on the Marshall–Lerner condition. [2]

items.stem: Sundara spends $120bn a year on imported consumer goods and has a current account deficit of $15bn. It imposes a 20% tariff on these imports. The price elasticity of demand for the imports is −2. Assuming the full tariff is passed on to consumers, calculate the percentage change in the volume of imports.

Classify each policy as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side, and explain how it could reduce a current account deficit. (i) Sundara imposes a 15% tariff on imported consumer goods. (ii) Sundara subsidises its exporters of car tyres. (iii) The central bank of Sundara devalues the naira by 10%.
items.answer: (i) Expenditure-switching policy: switches spending from imports to domestic goods. (ii) Expenditure-switching policy: lowers export prices so foreign spending switches to Sundara’s goods. (iii) Expenditure-switching policy: makes imports dearer and exports cheaper, switching spending to domestic output.
items.markingKey: (i) Expenditure-switching policy [1]; explanation [1] (ii) Expenditure-switching policy [1]; explanation [1] (iii) Expenditure-switching policy [1]; explanation [1] Total [6]

items.stem: The government of Jovania wants to reduce its current account deficit before the next election. Explain how expenditure-switching policies can be used to reduce a current account deficit.
items.answer: Tariffs, quotas, export subsidies, devaluation; change relative prices; Marshall–Lerner and J-curve; retaliation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Tariffs, quotas, export subsidies, devaluation; change relative prices; Marshall–Lerner and J-curve; retaliation. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: What is an expenditure-reducing policy?
options: A policy that raises export subsidies
A policy that reduces total spending in the economy, which reduces spending on imports
A policy that changes the relative price of imports
items.answer: A policy that reduces total spending in the economy, which reduces spending on imports
items.markingKey: Deflationary fiscal or monetary policy.

items.stem: Explain how contractionary fiscal policy can reduce a current account deficit.
items.answer: Higher taxes or lower government spending reduce AD and national income; with a marginal propensity to import, spending on imports falls; lower demand may also reduce inflation and improve competitiveness.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: AD/income fall; 1 mark: imports fall via mpm; 1 mark: lower inflation/competitiveness [3]

items.stem: Explain why expenditure-reducing policies may conflict with other macroeconomic objectives.
items.answer: Lower AD reduces growth and raises unemployment, because spending on domestic goods falls as well as imports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower growth; 1 mark: higher unemployment [2]

items.stem: The central bank of Zentara raises interest rates to reduce borrowing and spending. Which type of policy to correct a current account deficit is this?
items.answer: Expenditure-reducing policy
items.markingKey: Expenditure-reducing policy: lower consumption and investment reduce demand for imports.

items.stem: Classify each policy as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side, and explain how it could reduce a current account deficit. (i) Ostrelia introduces a quota on imported cars. (ii) Ostrelia cuts government spending on public sector projects.
items.answer: (i) Expenditure-switching policy: limits imports so spending switches to domestic cars. (ii) Expenditure-reducing policy: lower AD reduces income and imports.
items.markingKey: (i) Expenditure-switching policy [1]; explanation [1] (ii) Expenditure-reducing policy [1]; explanation [1] Total [4]

items.stem: Loristan has a current account deficit of 6% of GDP and unemployment of 9%. Explain how expenditure-reducing policies can reduce a current account deficit.
items.answer: Contractionary fiscal (taxes up, spending down) and monetary (interest rates up) policy; lower AD and income; mpm; lower inflation improves competitiveness.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Contractionary fiscal (taxes up, spending down) and monetary (interest rates up) policy; lower AD and income; mpm; lower inflation improves competitiveness. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Which is an expenditure-reducing policy?
options: An increase in income tax rates
items.answer: An increase in income tax rates
items.markingKey: Lower disposable income, lower imports.

items.stem: Explain why a small marginal propensity to import makes expenditure-reducing policies costly.
items.answer: If only a small share of each extra dollar of income is spent on imports, income must fall by a large amount to reduce imports significantly, causing large output and job losses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: small mpm means small fall in imports; 1 mark: large fall in income needed [2]

items.stem: To reduce a current account deficit of $10bn, the government of Esteria cuts its spending by $15bn. The multiplier is 1.5 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.25. Calculate the fall in national income.

Classify each policy as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side, and explain how it could reduce a current account deficit. (i) The government of Tarvia raises income tax rates to reduce consumer spending. (ii) The central bank of Tarvia raises interest rates to reduce borrowing and spending.
items.answer: (i) Expenditure-reducing policy: lower disposable income reduces total spending, including on imports. (ii) Expenditure-reducing policy: lower consumption and investment reduce demand for imports.
items.markingKey: (i) Expenditure-reducing policy [1]; explanation [1] (ii) Expenditure-reducing policy [1]; explanation [1] Total [4]

(b) Calculate the fall in national income needed to reduce imports by $6bn.

items.stem: Extract: Sundara has a current account deficit of 5% of GDP, unemployment of 4% and inflation of 10%. The finance minister proposes higher income tax to cut spending; the central bank prefers to let the kip depreciate; business leaders call for tariffs on imported consumer goods; economists argue that only supply-side reforms will solve the problem. The marginal propensity to import is 0.3. (a) Calculate the fall in national income needed to reduce imports by $6bn. (b) Explain which policy is likely to cause the greatest conflict with Sundara’s other macroeconomic objectives.
items.answer: (a) ΔY = 6/0.3 = $20bn. (b) Depreciation or tariffs: with high inflation, higher import prices would add to inflation.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: ΔY = 6/0.3 = $20bn. [2] (b) Credit: Depreciation or tariffs: with high inflation, higher import prices would add to inflation. [3]

items.stem: Which policy to reduce a current account deficit is most likely to conflict with low unemployment?
items.answer: Higher income tax rates
items.markingKey: Expenditure-reducing lowers AD and output.

items.stem: Explain why a policy to reduce a current account deficit may conflict with economic growth.
items.answer: Expenditure-reducing policies lower AD, reducing spending on domestic goods as well as imports, so real GDP growth falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower AD; 1 mark: lower growth/output [2]

items.stem: Explain why the effectiveness of policies to correct a current account deficit depends on its cause.
items.answer: A cyclical deficit from booming demand suits expenditure-reducing policy; a structural deficit from low competitiveness needs supply-side reform; an overvalued currency may need depreciation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cyclical vs structural; 1 mark: matching policy [2]

items.stem: Merania raises taxes to cut its current account deficit, and unemployment rises from 5% to 8%. Which outcome does this illustrate?
options: Conflict between the current account and employment
Conflict between the current account and price stability
items.answer: Conflict between the current account and employment
items.markingKey: Conflict between the current account and employment: lower AD cuts imports but also domestic output and jobs.

items.stem: Zentara raises taxes to cut its current account deficit, and unemployment rises from 5% to 8%. Which outcome does this illustrate? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Conflict between the current account and employment: lower AD cuts imports but also domestic output and jobs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Conflict between the current account and employment; 1 mark: explanation – lower AD cuts imports but also domestic output and jobs. [2]

items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Higher income tax: expenditure-reducing; depreciation and tariffs: expenditure-switching; supply-side reforms: supply-side. [2] (b) Credit: Higher income tax: with high unemployment, lower AD would raise unemployment further. [3]

items.stem: Explain why supply-side policies may be the most effective long-run solution to a current account deficit.
items.answer: They raise productivity and quality, lowering costs and improving price and non-price competitiveness, so exports rise and imports fall without reducing AD or raising inflation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: competitiveness; 1 mark: no conflict with growth/inflation [2]

items.stem: Ravi wrote in a homework answer: ‘Using higher interest rates to cut the current account deficit of Merania will also boost growth.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: Higher rates reduce consumption and investment, so AD and growth fall; there is a conflict of objectives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Higher rates reduce consumption and investment, so AD and growth fall; there is a conflict of objectives. [2]

items.stem: Westaria devalued the yuan by 15% at the start of year 1. Imports make up 20% of its consumer price index. Current account balance as % of GDP: year 0: −5%; year 1: −5.8%; year 2: −5.3%; year 3: −3.3%; year 4: −2.3% (year 0 is before the devaluation). Unemployment fell from 8% in year 0 to 6.5% in year 4. What does the pattern of the current account after the devaluation show?
options: The Marshall–Lerner condition was met immediately
items.answer: A J-curve effect
items.markingKey: The balance worsens in year 1 then improves: a J-curve.

items.stem: For each case, identify the outcome of the policy for macroeconomic objectives and explain it. (i) Umbria Nova raises taxes to cut its current account deficit, and unemployment rises from 5% to 8%. (ii) Umbria Nova raises interest rates to reduce spending on imports, and the currency appreciates, hurting exporters.
items.answer: (i) Conflict between the current account and employment (ii) Policy partly self-defeating
items.markingKey: (i) Conflict between the current account and employment – lower AD cuts imports but also domestic output and jobs. [2] (ii) Policy partly self-defeating – appreciation reduces export competitiveness. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: How does a tariff help to reduce a current account deficit?
options: It increases the price of exports
It increases the value of the currency
It raises the price of imports, so spending switches to domestic goods
items.answer: It raises the price of imports, so spending switches to domestic goods
items.markingKey: Expenditure switching.

items.stem: In a revision note Leila wrote: ‘An export subsidy is an expenditure-reducing policy.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: It lowers export prices to switch foreign spending towards domestic goods, so it is expenditure-switching.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It lowers export prices to switch foreign spending towards domestic goods, so it is expenditure-switching. [2]

items.stem: In a revision note Felix wrote: ‘Expenditure-switching policies work by reducing total spending in the economy.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: They change relative prices so spending switches from imports to domestic goods; reducing total spending is expenditure-reducing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – They change relative prices so spending switches from imports to domestic goods; reducing total spending is expenditure-reducing. [2]

items.stem: Merania spends $60bn a year on imported consumer goods and has a current account deficit of $8bn. It imposes a 15% tariff on these imports. The price elasticity of demand for the imports is −0.4. Assume the full tariff is passed on to consumers. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the volume of imports. (b) Calculate the new value of imports at world prices and the effect on the current account deficit.
items.answer: (a) Volume of imports changes by −0.4 × 15% = −6%. (b) Import spending paid abroad (at world prices) falls from $60bn to $56.4bn, a fall of $3.6bn; the current account deficit would fall to $4.4bn if nothing else changes.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) new imports [1]; new deficit [1] [3]

items.stem: Merania has a current account deficit, inflation of 2% and unemployment of 9%. Explain which type of policy would cause the least conflict with its other objectives.
items.answer: With low inflation and high unemployment, expenditure-switching (e.g. depreciation) raises net exports and AD, helping both the deficit and jobs; supply-side policy helps in the long run; expenditure-reducing would raise unemployment.

Conflict between the current account and price stability
items.answer: No conflict: supply-side improvement
items.markingKey: No conflict: supply-side improvement: higher productivity improves competitiveness without reducing AD.

items.stem: Lunaria devalued the yuan by 10% at the start of year 1. Imports make up 30% of its consumer price index. Current account balance as % of GDP: year 0: −5%; year 1: −6%; year 2: −5.5%; year 3: −4%; year 4: −2.5% (year 0 is before the devaluation). Unemployment fell from 9% in year 0 to 7.5% in year 4. Inflation was 3% before the devaluation. (a) Describe and explain the change in the current account. (b) Estimate the direct effect of the devaluation on inflation, assuming import prices rise by the full devaluation.
items.answer: (a) The deficit widened from 5% to 6% of GDP in year 1, then narrowed to 2.5% by year 4: a J-curve, as demand was inelastic in the short run and became more elastic later (Marshall–Lerner met). (b) Direct effect on inflation ≈ 30% × 10% = 3 percentage points, so inflation may rise from 3% to about 6%.
items.markingKey: (a) description [1]; J-curve explanation [1] (b) [2] [4]

items.answer: $5bn

items.stem: Marvona has a current account deficit of 6% of GDP and inflation of 9%. Explain why expenditure-reducing policies might be suitable.
items.answer: Lower AD reduces both imports and inflationary pressure; lower inflation also improves price competitiveness of exports, helping the current account.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reduces imports; 1 mark: also lowers inflation/improves competitiveness [2]

items.stem: Nordavia has a current account deficit and unemployment of 11%. Explain why expenditure-reducing policies might be unsuitable.
items.answer: Reducing AD would raise unemployment further and lower growth; expenditure-switching or supply-side policies would be less damaging.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher unemployment; 1 mark: alternative policy [2]

items.stem: Rovania introduces a quota on imported cars. Which type of policy to correct a current account deficit is this?
items.answer: Expenditure-switching policy
items.markingKey: Expenditure-switching policy: limits imports so spending switches to domestic cars.

items.stem: To reduce a current account deficit of $15bn, the government of Halvoria cuts its spending by $12bn. The multiplier is 2.5 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.15. Calculate the fall in national income.
items.answer: $30bn

items.stem: Extract: Pelora has a current account deficit of 5% of GDP, unemployment of 11% and inflation of 8%. The finance minister proposes higher income tax to cut spending; the central bank prefers to let the kwacha depreciate; business leaders call for tariffs on imported consumer goods; economists argue that only supply-side reforms will solve the problem. The marginal propensity to import is 0.25. (a) Classify each of the four proposals as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side. (b) Calculate the fall in national income needed to reduce imports by $6bn. (c) Explain how a depreciation could reduce the deficit, and why it might not do so at first.
items.answer: (a) Higher income tax: expenditure-reducing; depreciation and tariffs: expenditure-switching; supply-side reforms: supply-side. (b) ΔY = 6/0.25 = $24bn. (c) Exports cheaper, imports dearer; J-curve and Marshall–Lerner condition.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Higher income tax: expenditure-reducing; depreciation and tariffs: expenditure-switching; supply-side reforms: supply-side. [2] (b) Credit: ΔY = 6/0.25 = $24bn. [2] (c) Credit: Exports cheaper, imports dearer; J-curve and Marshall–Lerner condition. [4]

items.stem: Extract: Kestria has a current account deficit of 7% of GDP, unemployment of 4% and inflation of 2%. The finance minister proposes higher income tax to cut spending; the central bank prefers to let the yuan depreciate; business leaders call for tariffs on imported consumer goods; economists argue that only supply-side reforms will solve the problem. The marginal propensity to import is 0.3. (a) Classify each of the four proposals as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side. (b) Explain how a depreciation could reduce the deficit, and why it might not do so at first.
items.answer: (a) Higher income tax: expenditure-reducing; depreciation and tariffs: expenditure-switching; supply-side reforms: supply-side. (b) Exports cheaper, imports dearer; J-curve and Marshall–Lerner condition.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Higher income tax: expenditure-reducing; depreciation and tariffs: expenditure-switching; supply-side reforms: supply-side. [2] (b) Credit: Exports cheaper, imports dearer; J-curve and Marshall–Lerner condition. [4]

items.stem: Which policy is least likely to conflict with other macroeconomic objectives in the long run?
items.answer: Supply-side policies that raise productivity
items.markingKey: Shift LRAS right.

items.stem: Tomás wrote in a homework answer: ‘Using higher interest rates to cut the current account deficit of Zentara will also boost growth.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Higher rates reduce consumption and investment, so AD and growth fall; there is a conflict of objectives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Higher rates reduce consumption and investment, so AD and growth fall; there is a conflict of objectives. [2]

items.stem: Omar wrote in a homework answer: ‘Every policy to correct a current account deficit conflicts with low inflation.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Expenditure-reducing policies lower AD and so reduce inflation; it is expenditure-switching policies such as devaluation that tend to raise it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Expenditure-reducing policies lower AD and so reduce inflation; it is expenditure-switching policies such as devaluation that tend to raise it. [2]

items.stem: Korvia devalued the yuan by 10% at the start of year 1. Imports make up 30% of its consumer price index. Current account balance as % of GDP: year 0: −6%; year 1: −6.8%; year 2: −6.3%; year 3: −5.1%; year 4: −3.6% (year 0 is before the devaluation). Unemployment fell from 8% in year 0 to 6.5% in year 4. What does the pattern of the current account after the devaluation show?
options: The Marshall–Lerner condition was met immediately
items.answer: A J-curve effect
items.markingKey: The balance worsens in year 1 then improves: a J-curve.

items.stem: Istrana devalued the rupiah by 20% at the start of year 1. Imports make up 20% of its consumer price index. Current account balance as % of GDP: year 0: −5%; year 1: −5.5%; year 2: −5%; year 3: −3.8%; year 4: −2.3% (year 0 is before the devaluation). Unemployment fell from 10% in year 0 to 8.5% in year 4. Inflation was 4% before the devaluation. (a) Describe and explain the change in the current account. (b) Estimate the direct effect of the devaluation on inflation, assuming import prices rise by the full devaluation.
items.answer: (a) The deficit widened from 5% to 5.5% of GDP in year 1, then narrowed to 2.3% by year 4: a J-curve, as demand was inelastic in the short run and became more elastic later (Marshall–Lerner met). (b) Direct effect on inflation ≈ 20% × 20% = 4 percentage points, so inflation may rise from 4% to about 8%.
items.markingKey: (a) description [1]; J-curve explanation [1] (b) [2] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Merania has a current account deficit of 6% of GDP, unemployment of 11% and inflation of 8%. The finance minister proposes higher income tax to cut spending; the central bank prefers to let the rand depreciate; business leaders call for tariffs on imported consumer goods; economists argue that only supply-side reforms will solve the problem. The marginal propensity to import is 0.2. (a) Classify each of the four proposals as expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing or supply-side. (b) Discuss which policy the government should choose.
items.answer: (a) Higher income tax: expenditure-reducing; depreciation and tariffs: expenditure-switching; supply-side reforms: supply-side. (b) Compare effectiveness, time lags, conflicts with unemployment and inflation, retaliation, cause of the deficit; combination of policies; judgement.
